title: Micronet SDK sandbox-to-prod auth & multi-env quickstart
summary: AE + SE from Redwood walk Micronet through SDK quickstart in Python/TS, auth patterns for sandbox-to-prod, environment isolation, Redwood Console basics, and Optimize recommendations. Security questions on SSO/KMS and data residency; next steps include sandbox provisioning and a small smoke test POC.
next_steps: Alex Kim: provision sandbox Redwood account and share API keys & sandbox instructions (due: 2025-09-29)
Priya Shah: send sample Python+TS snippets for multi-env config and recommend batching settings
Micronet (Dana): schedule on-prem/private deployment discussion with infra team (target week of 2025-10-06)
action_items: Alex Kim: Create sandbox project, enable rate limits, attach sample dataset (due: 2025-09-29)
Priya Shah: Prepare a 20-min focused Optimize playbook tailored to Micronet traffic profile (due: 2025-10-02)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-25
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~57 minutes
Attendees: Alex Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Dana Lopez (Micronet CTO), Markus Eriksen (Backend), Lina Zhao (Security)

Summary (auto): Quickstart SDK integration; focus on auth patterns for sandbox->prod, environment variable patterns in Python/TypeScript, how to use Redwood Console to manage API keys and quotas, Optimize recommendations for batching and KV cache usage, and discussion of VPC/private deployment constraints for prod.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Alex from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with me is priya our solutions engineer, um we'll run through a short quickstart, try not to go too long, want to make sure we cover your auth and env questions for sandbox to prod migration
[00:18] Dana Lopez: thanks alex, excited, we just want something reproducible — we have a small microservice that will call the generation API and we want patterns for multi-env and secrets management
[00:30] Priya Shah: awesome, i'll share screen in a sec, real quick can you confirm you tried the public hosted api earlier or this is greenfield?
[00:38] Markus Eriksen: we played with a proof-of-concept using direct curl against a different provider, but we haven't integrated Redwood; we're interested in auth (api keys vs sso), rate limits, and how to separate sandbox/staging/prod keys
[00:50] Lina Zhao: and from security perspective, KMS integration and audit logs matter a lot, we also need an idea of data residency — do you store requests?
[01:05] Alex Kim: great, we'll cover all that — priya, maybe kick off with the SDK quickstart (python + ts) and then show the console for keys and projects
[01:12] Priya Shah: yeah, sharing now — alright i have the Redwood Console open, top-left is the project selector, we usually recommend one project per environment so "micronet-sandbox", "micronet-staging", "micronet-prod". that's helpful for quotas, and RBAC, and also for audit scoping
[01:36] Priya Shah: next pane is API keys, you can create environment-scoped keys. a common pattern is to store the key as a secret in your CI and in your environment manager: REDWOOD_API_KEY_SANDBOX, REDWOOD_API_KEY_STAGING, etc. then in code you pick the key based on NODE_ENV or a config map
[02:05] Markus Eriksen: can you show the python snippet? sometimes the ts example is more straightforward for our frontend, but backend is python
[02:12] Priya Shah: sure. python simple example: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); resp = client.generate(...). i'll paste exact snippet in the notes. for typescript it's very similar: new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
[02:32] Speaker 1: (mumble) and we also recommend using short-lived keys for higher privilege ops, that way you rotate more often —
[02:41] Dana Lopez: short-lived keys — do you mean session tokens or like ephemeral keys? how do we tie that into our SSO?
[02:49] Alex Kim: good q — we support SAML/SSO for Console access and you can integrate your identity provider for team access. for programmatic access you can create API keys via the Console or through our Admin APIs. we also support linking HSM/KMS for key wrapping if you go Private — priya can expand
[03:07] Priya Shah: yeah, for programmatic short-lived keys you can generate ephemeral tokens from a service that authenticates to Redwood using a long-lived key that's stored in a vault. alternatively if you use Redwood Private or have the VPC integration, you can enable customer-managed KMS and use envelope encryption so keys never persist unwrapped in Redwood's control plane
[03:32] Lina Zhao: how are logs handled? we need audit logs with request/response metadata, and we cannot store PII; is there a way to strip or redact in transit?
[03:42] Alex Kim: by default our hosted logs keep metadata and partial request info for observability, but we have retention options and masking rules. for regulated flows we recommend Private + customer side redaction, or configure the Console to not retain full payloads. we'll send our security docs — they include SOC2 scope, data flow diagrams
[04:05] Dana Lopez: that would be helpful yes
[04:09] Priya Shah: jumping back to env patterns — in a node lambda you'd map environment variables in the runtime and use the specific key for the environment. for dockerized python services, same env var approach; for k8s we recommend using secrets and mounting as env or file, and set RBAC so only deploy pipelines can access prod keys
[04:35] Markus Eriksen: ok makes sense. about quotas, can we throttle per-route, like for a customer-facing chat endpoint vs internal summarization?
[04:45] Priya Shah: yes, Console supports per-route quotas and token budgets and you can attach rate-limit policies. you can also use the SDK's client-side throttling to smooth spikes. plus Optimize will recommend batching windows for lower p99 latency vs throughput tradeoffs
[05:05] Alex Kim: let's demo a quick local dev flow — priya if you want to run the python sample and show the behavior switching keys between sandbox and prod
[05:13] Priya Shah: running now — i'm in a small sample repo; first: export REDWOOD_API_KEY_SANDBOX=sk_live_abc... then run python app.py --env sandbox. notice logs are prefixed with the project id micronet-sandbox and the Console shows a live request. switching to prod key, the project in the Console switches and quotas apply
[05:35] Priya Shah: i'll paste the commands. also note the SDK emits a request id header x-rw-request-id that you can echo in your logs for correlating with Console traces
[05:50] Markus Eriksen: ooh that request id will be handy for correlating with our distributed tracing
[05:55] Alex Kim: exactly, it helps with the per-token latency breakdown in Console tracing
[06:04] Dana Lopez: what's the suggested pattern for CI? do we inject prod key into pipelines or use a deploy-time service account?
[06:12] Priya Shah: good practice is to have your CI use a deploy service account which calls an internal token-exchange service that mints ephemeral keys for the specific deploy job. avoid storing prod keys in build logs. for quickstarts we give a sample GH Actions snippet that pulls a key from your vault and sets REDWOOD_API_KEY_PROD just for the deploy step
[06:33] Lina Zhao: security follow — if we go Private, does Redwood have an on-prem binary or is it a managed control plane with customer data plane?
[06:41] Alex Kim: Private is hybrid: control plane can be customer-managed and the data plane can be in your VPC or on-prem. for air-gapped customers we have an on-prem package. for cloud VPC deployments you can use private endpoints and FMC rules. we'll have SE docs for your infra team
[06:58] Priya Shah: want to switch to Optimize? i'll bring up the Optimize console. Optimize takes telemetry and suggests batching sizes, KV cache policies and quantization recommendations. for example, if your average prompt length is 120 tokens with many prefix tokens, Optimize might recommend increasing local KV cache TTL and enabling continuous batching windows of 30ms to improve throughput without hitting p99 latency SLOs
[07:28] Markus Eriksen: can Optimize recommend different quantization for different models? we use a mix of open weights and custom fine-tuned models
[07:36] Priya Shah: yes it can. Optimize profiles workloads per model and suggests quantization/variant (e.g., int8 vs int4) and routing policies. it also flags quality regressions via evals — if quantization causes a delta over your eval threshold it'll alert and suggest a fallback policy to a higher-precision variant
[07:58] Dana Lopez: is there a cost calculator? we have strict cost budgets for prod, would like ballpark monthly $ estimates if we move from provider X
[08:07] Speaker 2: (overlap) we have a cost estimator in the Console, you can project token volume and vCPU/GPU cost, and Optimize gives per-token unit economics when you enable telemetry
[08:20] Alex Kim: demo note — sometimes provider names get swapped in transcript; but yes we'll export a sample cost sheet after this call.
[08:28] Priya Shah: quick demo — here's the SDK config file pattern i recommend: config.yaml with env map pointing to project ids and keys. (shows file) envs: sandbox: project: micronet-sandbox key_env: REDWOOD_API_KEY_SANDBOX staging: project: micronet-staging key_env: REDWOOD_API_KEY_STAGING prod: project: micronet-prod key_env: REDWOOD_API_KEY_PROD
[08:58] Priya Shah: code then selects config[os.getenv('APP_ENV')].key_env to pick the right variable — trivial but prevents leaking prod to dev.
[09:08] Markus Eriksen: small question on caching: our summarization pipeline often repeats the same few prompts, is there a recommended local cache or do you recommend server-side caching?
[09:18] Priya Shah: both. local prefix caching reduces payload size and server-side KV cache in Redwood is great for shared results across services. we can set prefix-based cache TTLs; Optimize can recommend suitable TTLs after a short telemetry window
[09:34] Alex Kim: I'm going to show the Console's keys page: you can tag keys with "env:sandbox" etc. and create scoped keys limited to particular routes. that way you can issue a "summarize-only" key to a service without generation permission for other routes
[09:52] Lina Zhao: route-scoped keys look useful. for audit, can we append metadata which user created the key?
[09:58] Priya Shah: yes audit logs include creator, timestamp, and request metadata. we'll also surface which key was used for which request id in tracing
[10:10] Dana Lopez: any gotchas moving from sandbox to prod? timeline concerns?
[10:15] Alex Kim: three typical ones — 1) keys and RBAC: ensure prod keys are locked down and audited, 2) latency budgeting: prod SLOs often require Dedicated or region pinning to meet p99, 3) data residency/compliance — if you have strict policies you may need Private or VPC-hosted data planes.
[10:35] Markus Eriksen: about Dedicated — what's the threshold? we have bursts but stable baseline of 10 rps and spikes to 200 rps occasionally
[10:44] Priya Shah: Dedicated is usually recommended when sustained throughput and p99 latency guarantees matter; we can dimension a reserved GPU pool. autoscaling/burst capacity handles spikes but committed capacity is priced for baseline. Optimize can model your traffic and suggest reserved vs burst sizing
[11:02] Alex Kim: quick interjection — do you have an SRE or infra person we should loop in for the Dedicated sizing call?
[11:08] Dana Lopez: yes, that's markus, i'll cc him on followups
[11:12] Priya Shah: switching to the sample repo again — i'll show the typescript example for serverless frontends: import Redwood from '@redwoodai/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const resp = await client.chat.create({ model: 'rw-3-small', messages: [...] });
[11:38] Markus Eriksen: i noticed model names are rw-3-small in your sample — can customers bring custom fine-tuned models?
[11:45] Priya Shah: yes, you can onboard fine-tuned artifacts. onboarding includes a model manifest and perf profile; Optimize will profile and suggest kernels/quantization for the inference runtime. for private on-prem there are extra steps for artifact upload
[12:00] Lina Zhao: about model artifacts — are they encrypted at rest? and can we use our KMS?
[12:07] Alex Kim: artifacts are encrypted at rest. for Private we support customer-managed KMS; for hosted we manage keys but you can choose restricted retention and rotation policies.
[12:20] Dana Lopez: good. any limitations on sequence length or streaming? our use case uses long contexts sometimes up to 8k tokens
[12:28] Priya Shah: runtime supports long contexts; kernel selection adapts for longer sequences. streaming is supported and the SDK surfaces chunks. if you plan for persistent chat with KV cache, we'd recommend pinning a model variant compatible with your KV size and set the cache TTL accordingly
[12:48] Alex Kim: ok, quick pivot — let's do a live smoke test: priya will run a small batch of 10 concurrent requests to simulate staging load, then we'll show Console traces and p99 latency numbers
[12:58] Priya Shah: kicking off load now — you should see requests appear in Console. notice p50 is 80ms p95 180ms p99 340ms for the sandbox instance; Prod on dedicated should be better, but this gives a baseline
[13:22] Markus Eriksen: that's pretty decent. is there request-level token accounting we can push to our observability?
[13:30] Priya Shah: yes you can export per-request token usage via the telemetry API; some customers push this to a billing spreadsheet or internal metrics to track cost per feature
[13:45] Dana Lopez: one more question on env branching: we use feature branches and ephemeral preview environments; is there a recommended pattern for creating ephemeral keys?
[13:55] Alex Kim: ephemeral keys via your CI can be minted per preview and tagged with TTL; console supports short-lived keys or API to create keys programmatically which we can automate as part of your preview job
[14:09] Speaker 3: (background) oh and make sure your concurrency settings don't blow through your token quota — there are safeguards in Console to auto-throttle if a quota is exceeded
[14:20] Priya Shah: wrapping up the dev quickstart — i'll drop a zip of the sample repo, the exact python and ts snippets, and a GH Actions sample in the notes. also sending our Sandbox checklist which has config, secrets, and common gotchas
[14:35] Dana Lopez: great, what's the expected time to get a sandbox provisioned?
[14:40] Alex Kim: we can provision same-day for sandbox usually; for Private or Dedicated there's a sizing and procurement step which takes longer. i'll provision sandbox today and share keys by EOD if we have necessary contact info
[14:54] Dana Lopez: perfect
[15:00] Priya Shah: security quick checklist — SAML for team access, KMS options for key management, optional on-prem packages for PII flows, and audit logs with retention controls. we'll attach the security pack with SOC2 docs
[15:18] Lina Zhao: will do, we'll review and send any follow-ups.
[15:22] Alex Kim: ok final quick notes: we'll also schedule a follow-up to run a short perf test with your internal SREs and discuss Dedicated sizing if you want. dana, markus, lina — does next tuesday 10/7 work for a 45-min slot?
[15:34] Dana Lopez: that's fine, i'll confirm via email.
[15:38] Alex Kim: cool. thanks everyone, we'll share the repo, keys, security pack, and cost estimator. any last questions?
[15:44] Markus Eriksen: not from me, thanks for the walkthrough.
[15:46] Lina Zhao: all good.
[15:48] Alex Kim: great, talk soon. bye.

End of transcript.
